title: Looking for work as a disabled person? Recognize your strengths and find an accessible workplace
author: Erika Katzman
attribution: This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.
paras: Finding a job is challenging enough without having to contend with stereotypes about disability. Yet ableist assumptions — including the association of disability with “economic inactivity” — can shape how employers perceive you and your abilities.

What employers often overlook is how much skill it takes to navigate an inaccessible world. While that labour contributes to the hidden costs of living with disabilities, it can also develop abilities that are useful at work.
Recognizing those skills can help you communicate what you bring to a job. Understanding your rights and assessing an employer’s commitment to accessibility can help you find a supportive workplace.
The skills you are already using

For many people whose bodies and minds defy social norms, time is a precious resource. When you fit therapy sessions and specialist appointments around work, school or other commitments, you are constantly practising organization, scheduling and time management.

If you use paratransit, you may need to book rides days in advance. When something goes wrong — an out-of-service elevator or a rideshare driver who refuses to accommodate your service animal — you need to know how to find an alternative quickly. These experiences can involve contingency planning, effective communication and creative problem-solving.

If you live with chronic illness or another condition that affects your energy, you may have developed ways to manage limited resources. American writer Christine Miserandino’s popular “spoon theory” describes anticipating how much energy everyday tasks require and deciding how to allocate it strategically.

You might use speech-to-text software to reduce the physical effort of typing, set reminders to reduce the mental effort of remembering routine tasks or plan breaks around demanding activities. You may also have learned when and how to request assistance, delegate responsibilities or rest.
These strategies can draw on prioritization, adaptability and effective resource management. When seeking employment, consider how those skills relate to the roles you want to pursue.
Understanding your rights
Navigating the job market as a disabled person can bring additional responsibilities, too, from disclosing your disability to advocating for the access and accommodations you need.
In many jurisdictions, human rights laws entitle disabled employees to accommodations — reasonable adjustments that enable workers with different abilities to perform the essential duties of a job.

These protections are important, but requesting accommodations requires decisions about when and what to disclose, which can be emotionally exhausting and leave you vulnerable to stigma and discrimination.

If you experience discrimination, pursuing a rights complaint can bring further challenges. Both the experience itself and the process of seeking redress can take a toll, consuming emotional, cognitive, physical and financial resources.
Finding the right fit

Knowing your rights is important, but legal protections cannot guarantee you will feel supported at work. When deciding where to apply, look for clues about how a prospective employer approaches accessibility. An organization’s website, job postings and statements about mission, values and priorities can reveal its commitment to diversity and inclusion.

An absence of accessibility features or rights-affirming language may be a warning sign, but does not necessarily mean an employer will be unwilling to adapt. You might even find opportunities to highlight your knowledge of accessibility as an asset, particularly if an organization is beginning to adopt inclusive design.

As you move through the hiring process, pay attention to how the employer addresses accessibility in practice. If you have a more apparent disability or need to disclose a disability to discuss accommodations, consider how the employer responds. Is information about accessibility readily available? Are your requests taken seriously? Are practical solutions discussed?

If you choose not to disclose, you can still connect the skills you have developed through your experiences to the abilities listed in a job posting. Think about which are relevant to the role description and how you could demonstrate them through examples from work, education or everyday life.

Discussing experience-based strengths in a job application or interview can be challenging, especially if you’re unsure how an employer will respond to your disability. A mentor can help you identify transferable skills and communicate them effectively.

You might try to connect informally with someone who has a similar condition or works in a field that interests you, explore career coaching from people with lived experience of disability or seek the support of a disability doula.
What employers can do

Anti-discrimination and employment legislation provide essential protections, but policy measures alone have not eliminated harmful stereotypes and employment gaps. Employers can go further by adopting inclusive design practices that plan and provide for a range of access needs.

Greater sensory awareness and flexibility around timelines, for example, can help more people work effectively. Anticipating human diversity from the outset can improve workplace culture — not only for employees, but for clients as well — benefiting those who identify as disabled as well as those who don’t.

One practical step is to develop and implement a transparent accessibility policy that explains what supports are available, how to make requests and who is responsible for responding. Responsibility for accessibility and inclusion must be clearly assigned within employee role descriptions and supported with adequate time and other resources.

Responsibilities should also be shared among staff with diverse experiences and perspectives. Disabled employees bring firsthand knowledge of workplace barriers and the changes that can make work more accessible. But relying on a single disabled employee to represent an entire community overlooks differences in disabled experiences and how disability intersects with race, gender and other aspects of identity. It can also tokenize that employee and place an unfair burden on them.

There is no shortage of open-access resources to help organizations develop more inclusive workplaces. In addition to valuing the expertise of employees with lived experience, employers can also seek advice from disabled-led services.

Finding an accessible workplace shouldn’t depend on how much time and energy you can spend advocating for yourself. Employers can take proactive action, rather than relying on individuals to identify and overcome barriers.

No one should have to repeatedly disclose personal information, justify access needs or take on the extra work of making their workplace inclusive. Employers who accept responsibility for accessibility can reduce that burden, creating workplaces where you are enabled to do your best work and develop your career.

contend with.en: to have to deal with a difficult situation or problem
contend with.ex: Small brands often have to contend with rising fabric costs.

stereotypes.en: fixed, oversimplified ideas about a type of person or thing
stereotypes.ex: The campaign challenged stereotypes about older models.

stereotype.en: a fixed, oversimplified idea about a type of person or thing
stereotype.ex: There is a stereotype that designers never follow deadlines.

ableist.en: showing unfair treatment of or bias against disabled people
ableist.ex: The old hiring form contained several ableist questions.

assumptions.en: things accepted as true without proof
assumptions.ex: Her assumptions about the market turned out to be wrong.

assumption.en: something accepted as true without proof
assumption.ex: We made the assumption that customers wanted brighter colours.

economic inactivity.en: the state of being neither employed nor looking for work
economic inactivity.ex: Rates of economic inactivity rose sharply after the pandemic.

overlook.en: to fail to notice or consider something
overlook.ex: It is easy to overlook small stitching errors when you are tired.

navigate.en: to find a way through a difficult or complicated situation
navigate.ex: She helped me navigate the visa application process.

inaccessible.en: difficult or impossible to reach, enter or use
inaccessible.ex: The gallery was inaccessible to wheelchair users until last year.

defy.en: to not follow or fit expected rules or patterns
defy.ex: Her designs defy traditional ideas of menswear.

precious.en: very valuable and not to be wasted
precious.ex: Weekends are precious when you work long hours.

paratransit.en: special transport services for people who cannot use regular public transport
paratransit.ex: He books paratransit every Monday for his clinic visit.

accommodate.en: to provide what someone needs or allow for something
accommodate.ex: The studio can accommodate up to twenty people.

contingency planning.en: preparing alternative plans in case something goes wrong
contingency planning.ex: Good contingency planning saved the fashion show when the lights failed.

chronic illness.en: a disease that lasts for a long time or keeps returning
chronic illness.ex: Living with a chronic illness can make full-time work tiring.

anticipating.en: expecting something and preparing for it
anticipating.ex: Anticipating heavy traffic, we left an hour early.

anticipate.en: to expect something and prepare for it
anticipate.ex: We anticipate strong demand for the winter collection.

allocate.en: to give a share of something for a particular purpose
allocate.ex: The team decided to allocate more budget to sampling.

strategically.en: in a way that is carefully planned to achieve a goal
strategically.ex: The shop is strategically located near the station.

delegate.en: to give part of your work or responsibility to someone else
delegate.ex: A good manager knows when to delegate tasks.

prioritization.en: deciding which tasks are most important and doing them first
prioritization.ex: Clear prioritization helped us finish the lookbook on time.

adaptability.en: the ability to change to suit new conditions

disclosing.ex: He felt nervous about disclosing his salary.

disclose.ex: You do not have to disclose your age on the application.

advocating for.en: publicly supporting or asking for something
advocating for.ex: She has spent years advocating for fair wages in garment factories.

advocate for.en: to publicly support or ask for something
advocate for.ex: Students should advocate for better study spaces.

accommodations.en: changes made so that someone can work or study equally
accommodations.ex: The exam centre offered accommodations such as extra time.

accommodation.en: a change made so that someone can work or study equally
accommodation.ex: A standing desk was her only accommodation request.

jurisdictions.en: areas where a particular set of laws applies

jurisdiction.en: an area where a particular set of laws applies
jurisdiction.ex: This case falls outside the court's jurisdiction.

entitle.en: to give someone the right to have or do something
entitle.ex: Your ticket will entitle you to free entry to the museum.

reasonable adjustments.en: sensible changes an employer makes so a disabled person can work
reasonable adjustments.ex: The company made reasonable adjustments, such as flexible hours.

vulnerable.ex: New freelancers are vulnerable to late payments.

stigma.en: strong negative feelings society has about a condition or group
stigma.ex: There is still a stigma around asking for mental health support.

discrimination.en: unfair treatment of people because of who they are
discrimination.ex: The law protects workers from age discrimination.

redress.en: payment or action to correct a wrong
redress.ex: Customers sought redress after the delivery was lost.

take a toll.en: to have a harmful effect over time
take a toll.ex: Constant night shifts began to take a toll on his health.

cognitive.en: connected with thinking, learning and memory

prospective.en: likely to become something in the future
prospective.ex: We showed the portfolio to a prospective client.

commitment.en: a strong promise or dedication to something
commitment.ex: The brand showed real commitment to sustainable materials.

inclusion.en: making sure everyone is accepted and able to take part
inclusion.ex: The festival focused on inclusion for all ages.

warning sign.en: something that shows a problem may exist
warning sign.ex: Frequent staff turnover is a warning sign in any company.

asset.en: a useful or valuable quality or skill
asset.ex: Speaking three languages is a real asset in retail.

readily.ex: Spare buttons are readily available at the counter.

transferable skills.ko: 다른 분야에도 쓸 수 있는 역량
transferable skills.en: abilities that are useful in many different jobs
transferable skills.ex: Project management is one of the most transferable skills you can have.

lived experience.en: knowledge gained from personally living through something
lived experience.ex: The panel included people with lived experience of homelessness.

eliminated.ex: The new software eliminated most data-entry errors.

eliminate.ex: We want to eliminate waste from the cutting process.

from the outset.ex: From the outset, the project had a clear budget.

implement.en: to put a plan or system into action
implement.ex: The office will implement a four-day week next year.

transparent.en: open and easy to understand, with nothing hidden
transparent.ex: The brand is transparent about where its cotton comes from.

adequate.en: enough or good enough for a purpose
adequate.ex: Make sure you get adequate sleep before the test.

firsthand.en: gained by personal experience, not from others
firsthand.ex: She has firsthand knowledge of how factories operate.

intersects with.en: connects with and affects something else

intersect with.en: to connect with and affect something else
intersect with.ex: Class can intersect with gender in shaping career choices.

tokenize.en: to include someone only to appear diverse, not to value them
tokenize.ex: Brands should not tokenize models from minority groups.

burden.ex: Childcare costs are a heavy burden for young parents.

proactive.en: acting in advance to prevent problems
proactive.ex: Be proactive and back up your files every week.

justify.en: to give good reasons for something
justify.ex: It is hard to justify spending so much on one coat.

no shortage of.ex: There is no shortage of cafés in this neighbourhood.

pursue.en: to try to achieve or follow something over time
pursue.ex: She left her job to pursue a master's degree in Berlin.
